name: 40 Years of Promises
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: From Feynman's Chalkboard to Today: A Field That Has Always Been Almost Ready
lesson.summary: Stretching the three-to-five-year pattern across the full span from Feynman's 1981 proposal to the present shows a field that has been described as nearly practical for roughly forty years running, longer than most other major technology transitions have taken from concept to maturity.
lesson.body:
Richard Feynman's 1981 talk is the conventional starting point for quantum computing as a field, and measuring forward from it to the mid-2020s covers a span of roughly forty five years, commonly rounded down in popular writing to about forty. Comparing that span to other major computing transitions is instructive. The classical transistor was invented in 1947, and by the early 1980s, roughly thirty five years later, transistorized computers had already gone through mainframes, minicomputers, and the first wave of personal computers reaching millions of households. The internet's core protocols were standardized in the early 1980s, and by the early 2020s, a similar forty-year span, it had become a utility as unremarkable as electricity in most of the developed world. Quantum computing, on the same forty-year clock, has not yet produced a single widely deployed commercial application.

This comparison needs a fair caveat: quantum computing is arguably solving a harder engineering problem than either of those examples. A transistor is a solid-state device that, once manufactured correctly, behaves the same way every time under normal conditions. A qubit must be isolated from its environment closely enough to preserve delicate quantum superposition and entanglement, while still being controllable enough to manipulate on demand, a combination that fights itself by nature. It is entirely possible that quantum computing was always going to take longer than transistor electronics or networking protocols, simply because the underlying physics is less forgiving.

Still, the forty-year framing is useful precisely because it strips away the excitement of any single announcement and asks a blunter question: at what point does three to five years away, repeated across four decades, stop functioning as a genuine estimate and start functioning as a fixed rhetorical device, disconnected from the actual state of the underlying engineering? The three-to-five-year pattern chapter showed why individual instances of this claim keep recurring. Stacking those instances across Feynman's 1981 idea, Shor's 1994 algorithm, the 1998 to 2001 lab demonstrations, D-Wave's 2007 launch, Google's 2019 claim, and IBM's 2023 chip shows the claim being made at intervals of roughly five to ten years apart, essentially the whole life of the field, without the window ever visibly closing.

A useful contrast is nuclear fusion power, which has its own famous joke that commercial fusion is always thirty years away, a line that has been repeated since roughly the 1950s. Quantum computing's version of that joke uses a shorter number, three to five years rather than thirty, which paradoxically makes it sound more credible each time it is repeated, even though the pattern of non-arrival is structurally the same. A shorter stated horizon feels more scientifically precise and less like an obvious dodge, even when it is being reset just as regularly.

None of this settles whether quantum computing will eventually deliver on its promises; the underlying physics is sound, and hardware metrics like qubit count, gate fidelity, and coherence time have genuinely improved across this same forty-year span, even if usefulness has lagged behind them. What the forty-year framing does is set a baseline of patience and evidence required before accepting the next three-to-five-year claim at face value, which is the direct setup for the specific catalog of missed predictions covered next.
